title: SC26: The Biggest Little Quantum Show in the World - HPCwire
html:
SC26 has broken all kinds of attendance records, with nearly 24,000 attendees piling into the McCormick Center in Chicago for the annual supercomputing extravaganza. AI is the big driver this week, but quantum isn’t far behind. The big question is whether we’ll start seeing the promised benefits before the next quantum winter sets in.

“Whether you know it or not, you are attending the largest quantum computing conference in the world in terms of attendance,” said Bob Sorensen, who is the lead analyst for quantum at Hyperion Research. “The exploration phase of the HPC community has really begun in earnest.”

Most promising QC applications (Source: Hyperion Research)

SC26 organizers touted 55 quantum computing vendors at the six-day show, which would represent a majority of the QC companies in the world. Superconducting, trapped ions, neutral atom, photonics, quantum dots–they’re all represented at SC26, which has an entire area dedicated to the branch of computing, dubbed the Quantum Junction.

Sorensen shared his latest research on quantum during Hyperion’s annual update at SC. Those who managed to make it to the 7 o’clock breakfast meeting were treated to scrambled eggs and bacon, with a side of supercomputing and quantum.

Sorensen’s update was mixed. While QC isn’t delivering computational benefits in production today, there are signs that we will see it soon. The number of players in the game and the amount of money funding them has never been higher. But the sentiment on the quantum street has darkened a bit, and odds of another quantum winter appear to be growing.

First, the upside.

“You’re at a quantum conference, whether you know it or not,” Sorensen said. “And the reason that’s happening is because the sector is moving towards reaching a point of utility-class, fault-tolerant quantum systems. [They] are definitely on the horizon. We’re already starting to see use cases that demonstrate the utility of running particular jobs on quantum systems that meet their classical counterparts.”

Hyperion says the quantum computing market was worth $1.4 billion in 2025, and its forecast says QC will grow at a compound annual growth rate of about 30% to become a $3 billion business by 2028.

“Now, the interesting thing here is I don’t believe that number, because I think we’re going to start hitting a few interesting hockey sticks when it comes to the quantum computing space,” Sorensen says. “The first one is we’re going to start to see killer applications out there. Perhaps an optimization, perhaps in computational chemistry, advanced material design, and interesting front runner and interesting early entrant into this is organizations looking at solving linear solvers, quantum system dynamics, partial differential equations, kinds of things.

The second potential hockey stick is exploration on the cloud. The cloud is serving up a low-cost quantum playground where interested parties can explore all kinds of different modalities, Sorensen says. One can easily start out with superconducting qubits or neutral atoms and move to trapped ions or photonics at their heart’s content.

What users hope to get out of QC (Source Hyperion Research)

“There’s been a lot of experimentation,” he says. “Everyone in this room could be running a quantum program back in that hotel tonight for almost no money.”

Sorensen is bullish on the arrival of killer applications as fault-tolerant QC systems start to become commercialized. Experiments on private clouds that used to run $1,000 to $100,000 per month will become legitimate procurements that are worth tens or hundreds of million of dollars, he says.

“That’s going to really drive the sector along pretty enthusiastically,” the former IDC analyst says.

But there are also downsides to quantum.

For starters, the sector is heavily dependent still on outside dollars to sustain itself. About two-thirds of the QC companies that Hyperion surveyed have government-related partnerships within the past three years. The rest are leaning on venture capital to keep the qubits flowing.

“The bottom line here, though, is that is that quantum computing companies still are looking for support, technical and financial from government workers,” Sorensen says. “They’re not self-sustaining in terms of revenue yet. That’s going to come in the next few years. But the government activity is a critical supporter of the trajectory of quantum computing.”

Hyperion analyst Bob Sorensen

Taking money from the government is not all bad. For starters, you get access to technology and money, and Uncle Sam typically doesn’t get a stake. That’s not the same as when you take money from private investors, who definitely will take a stake. Sorensen encouraged QC companies to welcome dollars from governments, which typically have a long-term view and are interested in long-term benefits to their countries (only about 25% of QC companies globally are American, he says).

Sorensen says his sources indicate there are more than 100 QC companies globally, which is up from around 80 at this time last year. While more quantum startups may sound like a good thing, Sorensen takes a negative view of it.

“There’s not enough talent, there’s not enough end users, and quite frankly, there’s not enough money to go around,” he said. “The sector has to contract. It has to consolidate. It has to become more efficient. We could seriously lose 80 to 90 of those quantum computing companies that still have a vibrant quantum computing sector going forward.”

Sorensen fears that when QC companies go under, the market will overreact, and essentially throw out the quantum baby with the bathwater.

Lastly, Hyperion’s research indicates a souring mood in quantum. The percentage of people saying a quantum winter is “somewhat unlikely” dropped from about 26% in 2024 to about 14% last year. Similarly, the percentage of people saying a quantum winter is “somewhat likely” shot up from about 23% in 2024 to 34% in 2025.

Likliehood of quantum winter (Source: Hyperion Research)

“But there’s a universal truth in this: Every company thinks there could be a quantum winter coming, but every company thinks it’s not for them. It’s going to be the other guys,” Sorensen says. “So optimism abounds at the cellular level.”

The takeaway is this: People are still figuring out where quantum fits in, and it remains a work in progress. Quantum computing is not yet a commercially or scientifically viable type of computing at the moment, but there is great hope that it soon will be. Progress is being made in quantum error correction and the supporting technology needed to begin solving real-world problems is being developed.

“The key here is end users want to explore relevant use case potential. They’re not looking for real significant advantage right now,” Sorensen says. “They want to kick the tires on quantum computing. And most importantly, they want to understand where in their workload the performance gains could actually be realized.

“And so that’s the stage right now,” he continues. “That’s why this is the biggest project in the world. It’s because HPC users want to understand what quantum can bring to the table for them, and the necessary actions they need to take to integrate quantum computing into their existing classical hardware and software ecosystem.”
